question: Which method performs best on the same tasks, under the same rules?

steps.title: Fix the comparison
steps.text: Say what is being compared and why it matters, and whether you are a neutral party or the author of one of the methods.

quotes.text: The purpose of a benchmark is to compare, so the comparison that is at the heart of a benchmark must be clearly defined.
The purpose and scope of a benchmark should be clearly defined at the beginning of the study, and will fundamentally guide the design and implementation.

steps.title: Choose the tasks
steps.text: Pick datasets and tasks that represent real use, including some where the right answer is known.

quotes.text: The tests in the benchmark should be a representative sample of the tasks that the tool or technique is expected to solve in actual practice.
Simulated data have the advantage that a known true signal (or ‘ground truth’) can easily be introduced

steps.title: Include fairly
steps.text: Include the methods by stated criteria, baselines among them, and give each the same care in setting its parameters.

quotes.text: certain methods should not be favored over others through more extensive parameter tuning.

steps.title: Measure
steps.text: Score every method with the same metrics, chosen for what users need, and repeat runs where results vary.

quotes.text: Performance is not an innate characteristic of the technology, but is the relationship between the technology and how it is used. As such, performance is a measure of fitness for purpose.

steps.title: Renew the benchmark
steps.text: Keep changing the benchmark, or methods end up tuned to its particular tests rather than to the problem.

quotes.text: Continued evolution of the benchmark is necessary to prevent researchers from making changes to optimise the performance of their contributions on a particular set of tests.

overfitting-leakage.text: In practice, it is necessary to evolve benchmarks to prevent overfitting
